title: Review the change and the test that claims to prove it
summary: A test can show the right approver on screen even when the software never chose that person. A pull request is a proposal to change the shared code. On PR-42, a second developer checks who made the assignment before approving the change.
owner: The change author describes the proposal and repairs gaps. A peer who understands routing and has authority to approve the affected files makes the review decision.
inputs: Jira feature CC-123 and its two acceptance criteria, the agreed behaviors the change has to demonstrate
The proposed files, current test results and the review rules for main, the shared branch that receives accepted changes
steps: Read the purpose in CC-123. Open Files changed on PR-42 and follow an eligible request from submission to its first assignment.
Inspect who can record a decision and how the tests arrange the starting state. Open the checks on this version and compare what each result demonstrates with the claims in the description.
Submit the appropriate review decision. When the author updates the proposal, recheck the change, its tests and the impact on your earlier conclusions.

detail.title: Give the reviewer a place to start

blocks.value: Mark the proposal ready when someone else can follow one complete behavior. In GitHub the reviewer reads the diff, the comparison of changed lines between the author’s branch and the target branch. For a small change in this example, set aside about 20 minutes to read the code and tests together. Waiting for a reviewer, running checks and handling a second round add separate time.

blocks.caption: Illustrative description for PR-42
rows: Title
CC-123 · Assign eligible requests when they are submitted
Purpose
For Purchasing, use the configured approver when a request arrives. The person submitting it leaves the recipient blank.
Scope
Follow submission into the routing rule, then the assignment record. The approval path must still reject an unrelated employee and leave the request pending.
Evidence requested
Compare the first assignment actor and recipient with AC-01. For AC-02, inspect both the decision response and the stored request state. Open the current test run from Checks.
Review focus
Could these tests still pass if automatic assignment stopped working? The mapping in this proposal is test data. Check its source before interpreting a pass.

blocks.value: Start with the rule and its tests side by side. If an unrelated file rename or formatting sweep makes it hard to see which lines change behavior, ask the author to separate that work. Keep a changed rule together with the test that could catch its failure. A short diff that changes who can approve a request may take longer to review than a long mechanical edit.

detail.title: Who can approve these files?

blocks.value: A code owner is a person or team designated for particular file paths. For example, both the service and its tests can belong to the routing team. The repository administrator can require an owner’s approval on the target branch. Colleagues with read access can also review and comment, including a business analyst who knows how Purchasing chooses the approver.

blocks.caption: Illustrative .github/CODEOWNERS on main
blocks.value:
/src/routing/  @example/routing-reviewers
/tests/        @example/routing-reviewers

blocks.label: Tool behavior
blocks.value: GitHub uses the ownership file on the target branch. It requests an owner when a proposal affecting an owned path is ready for review. A team named as owner must be visible and have write access to the repository. Requiring its approval takes a separate branch setting.

blocks.label: Team policy
blocks.value: In this example main requires one approving review and code-owner approval for owned paths. One eligible owner other than the author can satisfy both. The administrator enables dismissal of stale approvals, so a push that changes the reviewed diff requires fresh approval.

detail.title: The test assigned its own approver

blocks.value: PR-42’s test fixture, the data and setup that prepare a test, assigns the expected recipient before submitting the request. Its final assertion only checks that someone is assigned. This can succeed when the application never ran the routing rule. The reviewer first follows the setup through the submission and points to the exact line that supplied the answer.

blocks.caption: Illustrative review thread on the assignment test
rows: Peer reviewer · Request changes
The fixture sets the recipient before submission. If the routing call disappeared, this assertion would still pass. Please start unassigned and check the actor and recipient on the first assignment.
Author · reply after updating

Removed the setup assignment. The test submits a fresh eligible Purchasing request and reads its first assignment. It expects routing-rule as actor and Purchasing approver as recipient. Disabling routing locally makes the revised test fail on the missing event.
Peer reviewer · Approve after rechecking
I followed the updated setup, both assertions and the new run. The unrelated employee’s decision test also checks that the request remains pending. This resolves my request for changes.

blocks.value: Use Comment for a question or suggestion that leaves the decision open. Use Request changes when the proposal still lacks necessary evidence. Under the example’s required-review rule, a change request from this eligible reviewer holds merge until addressed and cleared. Use Approve after inspecting the correction. A reply that says “fixed” tells the reviewer where to look. The approval records the independent decision.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.value: Ask what would make the test fail. Seeing the expected final value is convincing only when the test establishes how that value got there.

detail.title: Connect the review to the merge decision

blocks.value: After a correction, open the changes since the previous review and look for other edits in the same push. For example, a revised test can now prove who assigned the request while a change alongside it weakens the permission check. Reread affected behavior before resolving the thread. Treating a resolved conversation as an approval leaves the review requirement outstanding. Relying on an approval dismissed after a later edit can leave that edit unexamined.

Read the required results separately on the current proposal. For PR-42 they are unit tests, lint (checks of code conventions), new-line coverage (how many changed executable lines ran), quality gate (automated code-analysis conditions) and dependency review (changes to the software packages the service uses). The type check, which looks for inconsistent uses of data types, is informational. A supplemental database test can inform the peer’s decision. Neither that test nor an approval alone satisfies the five required results.

The developer moves CC-123 from In development to In review and verifies its development link opens PR-42 in the connected repository. Put the decision and correction on the PR where the changed lines and fresh run are visible. Keep CC-123 In review during a hold. This repair to a proposed test stays on the feature. CC-131 is the separate defect found during quality assurance on an earlier build.

detail.title: What transfers

blocks.value: In another review tool, record the criterion, the exact version someone inspected and why the revised observation would expose a broken implementation. Arrange for a second person with authority over the affected files to revisit that judgment whenever the proposal changes.

evidence: Keep the reviewed revision, request for changes, author’s reply, fresh test run and the eligible peer’s approval together on PR-42. The link from CC-123 lets the next reader recover that history.
example: The initial test can pass with its preassigned recipient. The corrected test observes which actor made the first assignment after a fresh submission and which approver received it.
failure: The reviewer requests changes and identifies the setup that supplied the answer. The author revises the test and returns it for independent review before merge.
measure: Sample approvals on updated proposals. Can a second reviewer find the setup, the observation that distinguishes success from coincidence and an approval that covers the final diff?

title: Test who actually receives a submitted request
summary: A buyer submits a request without choosing an approver. Can the reviewer see who received it, and whether the routing rule made the assignment? This check answers those questions by reading what the application saved.
owner: The developer supplies the check and investigates failures. The reviewer reads its evidence alongside the other results on the pull request (PR), the proposal to merge a change into the shared code.
inputs: The tested revision of PR-42 for CC-123, the application’s database setup instructions, its pinned test dependencies and a Linux continuous integration (CI) runner, the machine running the automated job.
A disposable PostgreSQL database (temporary storage for this test), a fictional unit-to-group mapping and the approved expected recipient for acceptance criterion AC-01.
steps: Start a fresh database service, apply the proposed application’s schema changes (updates to how tables and fields are organized), and load a purchasing unit and its approver mapping.
Send an eligible request through the normal submission operation. Read the first assignment event through a separate database connection.
Compare the event’s actor and recipient with the business expectation. Attach the result to PR-42, then dispose of the test database.
evidence: Preserve the run link, exact checkout, named test, expected and observed assignment, and failure stage. A setup error needs its own explanation because it leaves the business outcome unknown.
example: CC-123 requires automatic assignment at submission. A test that directly enters the approver can produce a convincing-looking result even if the application never runs the rule.
failure: The developer first checks whether the service became ready and whether the case reached its assertion. The reviewer holds the routing decision open until there is evidence from a clean rerun.
measure: Track time from a change to an actionable result. Separate minutes spent starting the database from time running the case, and count failures that disappear on a clean rerun without a code change.

detail.title: Where the database earns its place

blocks.value: A unit test can give the routing function a small mapping held in memory. An integration test exercises the connection between real components. Here the application reads a unit’s mapping from PostgreSQL, creates a request, then saves an assignment event that another connection can see. A defect in a database query, a column name or the point where the application makes its changes permanent can appear only when those components run together.

Run the example when a proposed change touches submission, the routing query or the database structure. Budget a few minutes on a Linux continuous integration (CI) runner before merge. Downloading a database image, starting its process, applying the schema and writing to disk all take time. Put this focused scenario beside the fast unit checks so the reviewer gets a useful discrepancy while the author still has the change in hand.

blocks.label: Team policy
blocks.value: This is a supplemental pre-merge example. The five required pilot checks on PR-42 are unit tests (small behavior checks), lint (code rules), new-line coverage (changed lines exercised), quality gate (code-analysis threshold) and dependency review (risks in changed packages). Type check is informational. The database result informs peer review. Requiring it for merge would be a separate repository decision.

detail.title: Give each test a clean database

blocks.value: The sample below is an excerpt for a separate pull-request workflow. A service container starts a real database server for this job. The repository supplies the locked dependencies, application migrations (versioned changes to the database structure) and the test module shown below. The runner needs read access to the code and permission to fetch the database image. The database user can create databases only within this disposable service. The example password belongs to the job’s throwaway database.

blocks.caption: Illustrative GitHub Actions job excerpt for the supplemental workflow
blocks.value:
jobs:
  check-routing-storage:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: local-test-only
        ports:
          - 5432/tcp
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres"
          --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 3s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: python -m pip install -r requirements-test.lock
      - run: python -m pytest -q tests/integration/test_assignment.py
        env:
          PYTHONPATH: src
          PG_ADMIN: postgresql://postgres:local-test-only@127.0.0.1:${{ job.services.postgres.ports[5432] }}/postgres

blocks.label: Tool behavior
blocks.value: GitHub Actions maps the container’s database port to an available host port for this runner job and removes the service when the job ends. The readiness probe checks whether PostgreSQL is accepting connections. The application’s tables and sample records still have to be created.

A pytest fixture prepares resources for a test and cleans them up afterward. Give each invocation its own database so a failed assertion, a repeat run or simultaneous tests cannot supply another test’s assignment. In this illustrative application, migrate uses the supplied connection details and applies the checked-out migrations. All application calls close their connections before returning.

blocks.caption: Illustrative pytest fixture in tests/integration/test_assignment.py
blocks.value:
import os
from uuid import uuid4

import psycopg
import pytest
from psycopg import sql
from psycopg.conninfo import make_conninfo

from routing.migrations import migrate
from routing.submissions import submit_request

@pytest.fixture
def database():
    admin_url = os.environ["PG_ADMIN"]
    name = "case_" + uuid4().hex
    target = make_conninfo(admin_url, dbname=name)
    ident = sql.Identifier(name)
    with psycopg.connect(admin_url, autocommit=True) as admin:
        admin.execute(sql.SQL("CREATE DATABASE {}").format(ident))
        try:
            migrate(target)
            with psycopg.connect(target) as seed:
                seed.execute(
                    "INSERT INTO unit_routing (unit, recipient) VALUES (%s, %s)",
                    ("Purchasing", "Purchasing approver"),
                )
            yield target
        finally:
            admin.execute(sql.SQL("DROP DATABASE {}").format(ident))

detail.title: Compare the first stored assignment with the agreed recipient

blocks.value: In this example the database assigns each saved event a unique, increasing sequence number within its request. Sorting that request’s rows by this value makes the first assignment unambiguous even if two timestamps have the same precision.

The expected recipient comes from the example’s approved purchasing scenario. Enter it as a fixed expectation independent of the application’s lookup. The fixture loads an input mapping, which a reviewer can compare with the business case. If the expectation were queried from whatever mapping happened to be loaded, the test could endorse the wrong group. The submission function below is the application entry point for synchronously routing a request. Its caller supplies a unit, requester and eligibility data, leaving assignment to the rule.

blocks.caption: Illustrative database-backed AC-01 test in the same module
blocks.value:
def test_first_assignment(database):
    request_id = submit_request(
        database, unit="Purchasing", requester="buyer-7", eligible=True
    )
    with psycopg.connect(database) as observer:
        first = observer.execute(
            """SELECT actor, recipient FROM assignment_events
               WHERE request_id = %s
               ORDER BY event_sequence LIMIT 1""",
            (request_id,),
        ).fetchone()

    assert first is not None, f"No assignment for request {request_id}"
    assert first == ("routing-rule", "Purchasing approver")

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.value: Read the first event for the returned request identifier. A later employee correction can make the final recipient look correct. The original actor and recipient show what happened on submission.

Pass this case only if an event exists for this request and its first actor and recipient both match. An empty result exposes a missing assignment or a change the application failed to commit. A different actor exposes manual assignment. This case exercises AC-01 for one eligible purchasing request. The separate authorization criterion AC-02 needs an attempted decision and a check of the resulting request state.

detail.title: A manual assignment made the old check look green

blocks.value: In the shared CC-123 example the old test fills in the assignee itself and then reads the value back. The test can execute the relevant lines and still leave the reviewer unable to tell who routed the request. Remove that write, leave the mapping in place and submit the request normally. One possible result on a broken revision is an empty event history. This diagnostic is illustrative and was never executed against PR-42.

blocks.caption: Illustrative failure excerpt for an unassigned submission
blocks.value:
FAILED tests/integration/test_assignment.py::test_first_assignment
E   AssertionError: No assignment for request demo-r17
E   assert None is not None

Start with the job’s health and migration steps. If they completed, inspect the test unit’s loaded mapping, the returned request ID and the application’s writes before changing the assertion. For a missing event caused by a skipped rule, repair submission so it invokes the rule and commits the assignment. Rerun against an empty database. For a service-start failure, the CI maintainer checks the port and health output and reruns the same revision before drawing a conclusion about routing.

On Jira work item CC-123 add web links to PR-42 and the relevant job run. Record AC-01, the revision actually tested, the observed failure and the clean rerun when available. Keep CC-123 In review while the reviewer assesses the proposal. Two errors obscure the decision: accepting the most recent event can conceal a wrong first assignment, and carrying old rows into a rerun can make a broken write appear successful. The later qa-204 record concerns the built candidate in QA. It supplies no result for this supplemental job.

detail.title: What transfers

blocks.value: With Testcontainers for Python, the test process can start a separate PostgreSQL container and obtain its connection URL. For Psycopg, use PostgresContainer with driver=None to get a compatible URL. Keep the independent expected recipient, fresh connection and first saved event when changing how the database starts.

title: Decide whether PR-42 can enter main
summary: Someone has approved the routing change, but another change may have entered the shared code since they looked. Before bringing the two together, the team checks which version passed and whether the approval still counts. The build team then needs the exact version that entered the shared code.
owner: The repository administrator sets the rules. A developer with write access examines the result and merges an eligible proposal. The build maintainer receives the integrated source version.
inputs: Pull request PR-42, the proposal for feature CC-123, and its target main, the shared branch of the source repository
The current approval, named check results, and branch protection, the rules GitHub applies when someone updates main
steps: Open the merge panel on PR-42. Compare the outstanding requirements with the rule for main. Inspect the identity of the tested version and the source of each result.
If main has advanced, bring the proposal up to date under the example’s strict rule. Collect fresh results and any newly required review.

After merge, read the integrated commit (the saved version that entered the shared branch) from the merge record and confirm that the build used it. Attach the build record and image identifier to CC-123 before the handoff to quality assurance (QA).

detail.title: Read the rule that applies to main

blocks.value: A commit is an identified version of the source and its history. The head is the most recent commit on the proposal branch. The base branch is the target that will receive it. Opening the merge panel shows the requirements for the current proposal. GitHub reevaluates them as reviews, check results and branch updates arrive. Allow minutes for a new round of checks in this small example, plus the wait for an available machine or reviewer.

blocks.caption: Illustrative repository settings for the target branch
rows: Review before merge
Require a pull request and one approval. A change to an owned path requires an eligible code owner, a reviewer designated for that path. A single independent owner may meet both conditions.
Fresh approval
Dismiss stale approving reviews when the diff, the set of changes reviewed, changes. Have the owner inspect the revised proposal.
Required status checks
unit tests · lint · new-line coverage · quality gate · dependency review. Select the matching check names. Keep names distinct across workflows. The next section explains what each check tests.
Additional evidence
type check is visible and informational. The supplemental database integration example informs the reviewer. Neither is selected in the required list.
Current target
Enable the strict option requiring the branch to be up to date. In this example the author updates the proposal before another merge attempt.
Enforcement
Apply the rule to administrators as well, with no routine bypass. The person merging needs write permission. An eligible maintainer investigates a stuck rule.

blocks.label: Team policy
blocks.value: The administrator chose these five required results, the review settings and the strict update rule for this example. Inspect the effective rule on the intended target when working in an actual repository.

detail.title: What does each required result establish?

blocks.value: Start at the current pull request run. Unit tests exercise isolated behaviors. Lint checks the code against formatting and static rules. Both use the temporary test merge here, a snapshot combining the proposed changes with the target as it stood for that run. The new-line coverage check uses the unit run’s execution report and the changed executable lines. For this service the maintainer requires at least 80% of those lines to have run.

The quality gate uses SonarQube, the team’s code analysis service, to check the proposal against the target, including a condition on new bugs. Dependency review examines packages introduced or changed by the proposal and holds a newly introduced vulnerability of High or Critical severity under the example policy. Follow each result to the inputs it actually compared. An informational type check may deserve a repair even though its failure alone leaves the merge rule satisfied.

blocks.label: Tool behavior
blocks.value: GitHub branch protection can accept a successful, skipped or neutral check. A required workflow that never reports leaves the requirement outstanding. Look into an unexpected skip to find out whether the intended examination ran.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.value: A passing result covers the code and conditions that produced it. To evaluate a new combination of changes, collect evidence for that combination.

detail.title: An approval and four passes still leave PR-42 blocked

blocks.caption: Illustrative merge-panel reading for an intermediate PR-42 update
blocks.value:
Review: approved by an eligible routing owner
unit tests: passed
lint: passed
new-line coverage: failed — 31 of 50 new executable lines ran (62%)
quality gate: passed
dependency review: passed
type check: passed (informational)
Decision under the example rule: merge blocked

The author first opens the failing coverage check and finds the changed lines that did not run. If the denominator remains 50, at least 40 must run to meet the rule. Cover meaningful cases and check the outcome of each. A test that sets the approver before submission can inflate the count while missing the failure CC-123 exists to prevent. Push the revised tests to PR-42 and inspect the fresh result. Preserve the earlier failure so the reviewer can see what changed.

Suppose another proposal lands on main during that repair. Under the strict rule, update the branch against the new main and inspect any conflicts in routing or authorization. Verify the new run and reopen the review panel. When the reviewed changes have changed, stale approval dismissal requires a fresh decision by an eligible reviewer. Copying the old run link into a comment leaves the required check for the new version outstanding.

Keep CC-123 In review. The development link should open PR-42, where both the failed and later qualifying runs can be inspected. The developer handles the coverage repair. If a required result remains missing, the workflow maintainer checks the event, job name and reported revision before the repository administrator considers a rule change.

detail.title: How would a merge queue handle a busy target?

blocks.value: A merge queue takes eligible proposals in order and tests a temporary combination of the latest target branch and proposals ahead in line. It is an alternative to repeatedly updating the author’s branch by hand. GitHub offers queues for public repositories owned by organizations and for private organization repositories on GitHub Enterprise Cloud. An administrator configures the target and the queue’s merge method.

To adopt a queue, each GitHub Actions workflow providing required checks must also listen for merge_group, the event requesting checks on the queued combination. A workflow that listens only for pull_request will leave the queue waiting for its missing result and the merge will fail. A check written for one pull request may also expect fields or comparison inputs that the group event does not provide. Adapt those checks and verify all five required names report meaningful results for the queued version before enabling the rule. The PR-42 example uses the strict branch setting.

detail.title: Which commit does the build use?

blocks.caption: GitHub merge methods and the identity on main
columns: History and the commit to build
rows: Merge commit
Adds a commit joining the previous main and proposal histories. The original proposal commits keep their identities. Build the new merge commit.
Squash and merge
Combines the proposal’s changes in one new commit on main. The pull request keeps the individual review commits. Build the new squash commit.
Rebase and merge
Replays the proposal’s changes as individual commits on main without a separate merge commit. GitHub gives the replayed commits new identities. Build the last integrated commit for the proposal.

blocks.value: Read the integrated commit from the actual merge record and the revision checked out by the build. Copying the proposal head into the handoff can identify a different source version under any of these methods. The fictional qualification record identifies the integrated commit for PR-42 as 3ab862bc3190549bff7df2e0c1a02c9cc11459e4. It does not specify the earlier PR head or which merge method produced that result.

The next job packages that source in build-418. The developer records the integrated commit and the published image digest, the content identifier used to retrieve the exact package, on CC-123 and moves the feature to Ready for QA. The independent qualification on that image is qa-204. The earlier defect CC-131 has its own history on build-412 and build-415.

detail.title: What transfers

blocks.value: On another platform, find the target’s actual merge rules, the authority behind each approval and the version each required result inspected. Hand the build system the integrated source identifier and keep the link back to the proposal so a later reviewer can reconstruct both decisions.

evidence: The merge record ties PR-42 to the integrated commit. The build receipt ties that commit to build-418 and its published image digest.
example: The reviewer can approve the routing behavior while a required coverage check reports 62% against an 80% minimum. The author must repair the failed check and meet the other current requirements.
failure: A missing required result, failed check, stale approval or out-of-date branch holds merge under the example settings. Read the specific unmet requirement to identify who can clear it.
measure: Sample merged proposals and trace each one back from its build receipt to the integrated commit, the reviewed change and the applicable check runs. Track time waiting for a branch update separately from time spent fixing failures.

title: Build the exact image QA will test
summary: After a change joins the shared code, the team packages the application for testing. The build receipt gives quality assurance (QA) a way to check that the package they start is the one the developer handed over.
owner: The build maintainer publishes the image, a package containing the program and its runtime files. The developer links the receipt to the feature. The quality assurance (QA) lead verifies the identity and configuration of the running candidate.
inputs: The integrated commit (the saved source revision on the shared branch), the Dockerfile build instructions, locked dependencies and the target operating system and processor architecture.
A Linux build runner, a registry (the service that stores images), permission to read the source and publish the image, and registry read access for QA.
steps: Build from the integrated commit and publish the candidate for linux/amd64, meaning Linux on the 64-bit x86 architecture.
Capture the registry digest, a content fingerprint, from the push result. Inspect what it identifies and retain the build records.
Give QA the registry reference by digest, the platform and the build link. Check the running candidate and configuration before attributing a test run to it.
evidence: The build receipt pairs PR-42 with the integrated commit, build-418, the full published digest and linux/amd64. QA can follow the same candidate reference to its own environment record.
example: The fictional qualification record links build-418 to QA revision qa-r17, configuration qa-routing-3 and test run qa-204. A successful push alone says nothing about whom the service assigns.
failure: If the source, published object or running platform differs from the receipt, hold the handoff. The build maintainer reconciles the build and registry records with QA before testing resumes.

detail.title: What goes into the package?

blocks.value: Start when the reviewed change lands on the shared main branch. In the example a push triggers the main-release-build workflow on a Linux runner. Allow several minutes to download the base image, install dependencies, assemble the application and upload the result. A cold download or generating an inventory can dominate that time. Record the actual run duration separately from time waiting for a machine. The commit recorded for this step is the integrated revision. A pull request’s earlier proposed revision may have a different identifier.

The build context is the directory of files available to the builder. Here the checked-out project contains a routing Python module and requirements.lock listing exact package versions and accepted file hashes. The first stage collects the matching installable packages, called wheels. The second stage starts from the same Python base, installs those packages offline, and copies only the application. The team supplies a reviewed base-image reference pinned by digest, so a change behind a friendly base tag cannot silently alter these stages.

blocks.caption: Illustrative two-stage Dockerfile for a Python routing service
blocks.value:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
ARG PYTHON_BASE
FROM ${PYTHON_BASE} AS wheels
WORKDIR /deps
COPY requirements.lock .
RUN python -m pip download --only-binary=:all: --require-hashes \
    --dest /wheels -r requirements.lock

FROM ${PYTHON_BASE} AS runtime
WORKDIR /srv
COPY requirements.lock .
RUN --mount=type=bind,from=wheels,source=/wheels,target=/wheels \
    python -m pip install --no-index --no-cache-dir --require-hashes \
    --find-links=/wheels -r requirements.lock
COPY src/routing/ ./routing/
USER 65532:65532
CMD ["python", "-m", "routing"]

detail.title: Read the push result from the integrated build

blocks.value: This job is a proposed implementation. Set ROUTING_IMAGE to the lowercase Docker Hub repository name and PYTHON_BASE to the complete Python base reference including its verified digest. The example uses a Docker Hub access token with write permission for that repository. Store it as an Actions secret for the trusted build on main. QA receives separate read access. An image tag is a human-readable name pointing to an image and can move when another build publishes to it. Keep the build number for navigation and take the content fingerprint from the publish step itself.

blocks.caption: Illustrative main-release-build workflow with a publish step
blocks.value:
name: main-release-build
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.sha }}
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          username: ${{ vars.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        id: publish
        with:
          context: .
          build-args: PYTHON_BASE=${{ vars.PYTHON_BASE }}
          platforms: linux/amd64
          tags: ${{ vars.ROUTING_IMAGE }}:build-${{ github.run_number }}
          push: true
          sbom: true
          provenance: mode=min
      - name: Inspect the published object
        env:
          IMAGE: ${{ vars.ROUTING_IMAGE }}
          DIGEST: ${{ steps.publish.outputs.digest }}
        run: docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE@$DIGEST"

detail.title: Which digest should QA compare?

blocks.value: A manifest describes one runnable image and identifies its configuration and layers. An image index lists other manifests and the platforms they target. A registry’s published digest can therefore identify an index or an individual manifest. Inspect the exact published reference. For an index, find its runnable linux/amd64 entry and record that child manifest’s digest alongside the index digest. Attestation manifests can appear with platform unknown/unknown. They carry statements about the build and cannot run the application.

blocks.label: Tool behavior
blocks.value: Docker BuildKit, the build engine, can attach attestations to an image index even when it contains only one runnable platform. Inspect the manifest’s platform and its relationship to the index before comparing a platform digest reported by a runtime with the top-level push digest.

If the published object itself is a single image manifest, inspect its image configuration to confirm the operating system and architecture. In QA, read the running workload’s image identity and determine what kind of object its runtime exposes. Compare like with like, resolving the index to its child when needed. A local image configuration identifier can also differ from a registry manifest digest. If the runtime evidence cannot be related to the receipt, pause the handoff until the platform owner can explain the relationship.

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.value: An immutable image fixes the contents of the package. Routing also depends on the environment’s group mapping. Record the running image identity and the active configuration so another person can reconstruct the conditions of the test.

detail.title: What the additional build records tell you

blocks.caption: Three different questions about one candidate
rows: Image vulnerability scan
Which installed components match known vulnerability advisories at scan time?
Exact runnable platform digest, scanner version, report timestamp and the team’s findings policy.
Software bill of materials (SBOM)
Which components and versions did the inventory generator identify?
The attestation subject identifying the platform image being inventoried.
Build provenance
What source, builder and build inputs did the builder report?
The statement’s subject, the build run and the recorded commit, with detail depending on provenance mode and build context.

blocks.value: For example, an operator with Docker Scout configured can scan the published candidate using the platform setting shown below and retain the resulting report. An SBOM remains an inventory if a new vulnerability is disclosed tomorrow. A newer scan can evaluate that inventory against updated advisories. Provenance records origin information and still needs a trust decision about the builder. The fictional qualification record supplies neither a vulnerability verdict nor a verified attestation.

blocks.text_equivalent: PR-42’s integrated commit feeds build-418. The build publishes a digest and identifies linux/amd64 as the platform. QA verifies the running digest and configuration qa-routing-3 on qa-r17 before associating the candidate with qa-204.

detail.title: A tag points to the earlier repair

blocks.value: The shared case has three increments. PR-40 produced build-412, which failed the authorization case in qa-196. PR-41 produced build-415. Its retest in qa-198 verified the repair and closed defect CC-131. PR-42 then produced build-418, which needed an independent run on its own digest. Suppose a QA operator selects a tag still pointing to the repair image. The application may start normally and the repaired case may succeed, yet this tells the reviewer nothing about the later integrated candidate.

The build maintainer first resolves both published references and checks the platform. If this is the older build, QA selects build-418 by digest, checks the running revision and its configuration, and takes fresh observations. Preserve the mismatched attempt as such. Rebuilding from the same commit as a shortcut can introduce different input bytes and generate a new digest. Comparing an index digest directly to a child manifest can also create a false mismatch and waste a valid candidate.

blocks.label: Team policy
blocks.value: The developer moves CC-123 to Ready for QA when the integrated commit and the published candidate for linux/amd64 can be traced to build-418. Add web links to PR-42 and the build receipt on the Jira issue. A missing or mismatching candidate holds this handoff. The QA lead records the runtime verification and test run separately.

For the accepted fictional candidate, the qualification record names qa-r17, qa-routing-3 and qa-204 for AC-01 and AC-02. That record is the evidence for the observed routing behavior. The proposed tag mismatch and scan example are teaching examples without recorded outcomes.

detail.title: What transfers

blocks.value: Docker Buildx also provides the build command directly, accepting a Dockerfile, build context, platform, push destination and metadata-file path in place of the GitHub action’s inputs and digest output. On any build service, pass the published identity and platform forward, check the runtime’s actual selection and keep the scan, inventory and provenance attached to the object each describes.
